newsitem.title: JAPAN: Crudes ease in Asia on imminent Iraq oil shipments.
newsitem.headline: Crudes ease in Asia on imminent Iraq oil shipments.

text.p: Crude oil prices in Asia fell on Monday on expectations that limited Iraqi oil sales would resume soon, but traders and analysts said the dip was likely to be brief.
They said strong seasonal demand was likely to absorb the extra supplies.

"The resumption of Iraqi oil exports is certainly not bullish for the market. However, the market has already factored in the availability of Iraqi crude," said Akio Shibata, general manager of Marubeni Corp's Industrial Research Section.

U.N. officials said on Friday that, barring last-minute obstacles, U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali would be ready to give the go-ahead on Monday for the implementation of the Iraqi oil-for-food deal at a minute after midnight Eastern Standard Time.

Iraq last month accepted all U.N. conditions for it to be allowed to make oil exports worth $2 billion every six months to enable it to buy food and medicine for its sanctions-hit civilian population. The deal is renewable.
The exports, tightly supervised by the United Nations, would be Baghdad's first since a ban on oil exports from Iraq was imposed after its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
By 0630 GMT on Monday, benchmark January North Sea Brent futures prices on the Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX) had not been traded but were bid and asked at $24.20/24.45.
On Friday in London, the contract settled at $24.54.

The New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) January crude oil futures, another benchmark, were last traded in Asian hours on the after-hours ACCESS screen-based system at $25.42 per barrel. In New York on Friday, the contract settled at $25.62.
Traders and analysts agreed that the market could easily absorb Iraqi crude, as the exports were likely to coincide with peak demand in the northern winter.

"The dip in prices is probably just temporary," a crude trader said. "The impact of Iraqi oil exports may dent the market in the spring when demand starts to ease, but at the moment, futures prices are not likely to buckle easily," he said.

Iraqi Oil Minister Amir Muhammad Rasheed said on Friday that oil exports would begin on Tuesday. But U.N. spokeswoman Sylvana Foa doubted this would be the case as New York-based oil experts or overseers had up to 24 hours to review all contracts.

Traders said news on Friday that oil workers in France had called off a nine-day strike at Elf Aquitaine after accepting more pay and earlier retirement, while admitting defeat in a battle to save more jobs, also weighed on the market.
"The market seems to be interested in fresh factors, rather than news about Iraq," an official with a refiner said.
Marubeni's Shibata said he expected NYMEX light crude prices to stay within a range of $23.00-26.00 next year.
"Iraqi oil exports may pressure the price ceiling lower, however, the upward trend in prices since 1994 is not expected to stop," he said.

He said a combination of factors would prevent oil prices from tumbling. These included efforts by Western oil companies to reduce oil stock levels to cut costs and the possibility of political instability in the Middle East.
